claim: Small changes of Na/K pump activity regulate internal Ca release in cardiac myocytes via Na/Ca exchange.
source: Small changes of Na/K pump activity regulate internal Ca release in cardiac myocytes via Na/Ca exchange.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact, supported by citations in the introduction (Reuter et al., 2002; Hilgemann, 2004).

claim: Transient elevations of cytoplasmic Ca strongly regulate cardiac Na/K pumps.
source: We now show conversely that transient elevations of cytoplasmic Ca strongly regulate cardiac Na/K pumps.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 6-10.

claim: When cytoplasmic Na is submaximal, Na/K pump currents decay rapidly during extracellular K application.
source: When cytoplasmic Na is submaximal, Na/K pump currents decay rapidly during extracellular K application and multiple results suggest that an inactivation mechanism is involved.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B and throughout the manuscript.

claim: Multiple results suggest that an inactivation mechanism is involved in Na/K pump current decay.
source: When cytoplasmic Na is submaximal, Na/K pump currents decay rapidly during extracellular K application and multiple results suggest that an inactivation mechanism is involved.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2-4.

claim: Brief activation of Ca influx by reverse Na/Ca exchange enhances pump currents.
source: Brief activation of Ca influx by reverse Na/Ca exchange enhances pump currents and attenuates current decay, while repeated Ca elevations suppress pump currents.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6-8 with experimental data.

claim: Brief activation of Ca influx by reverse Na/Ca exchange attenuates pump current decay.
source: Brief activation of Ca influx by reverse Na/Ca exchange enhances pump currents and attenuates current decay, while repeated Ca elevations suppress pump currents.
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figures 6-8.

claim: Repeated Ca elevations suppress pump currents.
source: Brief activation of Ca influx by reverse Na/Ca exchange enhances pump currents and attenuates current decay, while repeated Ca elevations suppress pump currents.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8C and Figure 10A.

claim: Pump current enhancement by Ca elevation reverses over 3 min.
source: Pump current enhancement reverses over 3 min, and results are similar in myocytes lacking the regulatory protein, phospholemman.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6A and other experimental records.

claim: Results are similar in myocytes lacking the regulatory protein, phospholemman.
source: Pump current enhancement reverses over 3 min, and results are similar in myocytes lacking the regulatory protein, phospholemman.
evidence: This is documented in Table 1 with data from PLM-/- mice.

claim: Classical signaling mechanisms, including Ca-activated protein kinases and reactive oxygen, are evidently not involved in Ca-dependent pump regulation.
source: Classical signaling mechanisms, including Ca-activated protein kinases and reactive oxygen, are evidently not involved.
evidence: This is supported by extensive experimental testing documented in Table 1.

claim: Electrogenic signals mediated by intramembrane movement of hydrophobic ions increase and decrease in parallel with pump currents.
source: Electrogenic signals mediated by intramembrane movement of hydrophobic ions, such as hexyltriphenylphosphonium (C6TPP), increase and decrease in parallel with pump currents.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 10-12.

claim: Transient Ca elevation and Na/K pump inactivation cause opposing sarcolemma changes that may affect diverse membrane processes.
source: Thus, transient Ca elevation and Na/K pump inactivation cause opposing sarcolemma changes that may affect diverse membrane processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of membrane probe behavior in Figures 10-12.

claim: Na/K pumps establish the Na and K gradients used for ion transport and electrical signaling in animal cells.
source: Na/K pumps establish the Na and K gradients used for ion transport and electrical signaling in animal cells (Skou, 1990), thereby accounting for a large fraction of total energy expenditure (Milligan and McBride, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Na/K pumps account for a large fraction of total energy expenditure in animal cells.
source: Na/K pumps establish the Na and K gradients used for ion transport and electrical signaling in animal cells (Skou, 1990), thereby accounting for a large fraction of total energy expenditure (Milligan and McBride, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In cardiac myocytes, small changes of pump activity have large effects on excitation-contraction coupling by shifting the energetic equilibrium of Na/Ca exchangers.
source: In cardiac myocytes, small changes of pump activity have large effects on excitation-contraction coupling by shifting the energetic equilibrium of Na/Ca exchangers (Reuter et al., 2002; Hilgemann, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phospholemman can inhibit Na/K pumps with analogy to phospholamban action at SERCA Ca pumps.
source: The FXYD protein, phospholemman, can inhibit Na/K pumps with analogy to phospholamban action at SERCA Ca pumps, and this inhibition is proposed to be released when phospholemman is phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinases (PKAs) (Bibert et al., 2008; Han et al., 2010; Mishra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Phospholemman inhibition is proposed to be released when phospholemman is phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinases (PKAs).
source: The FXYD protein, phospholemman, can inhibit Na/K pumps with analogy to phospholamban action at SERCA Ca pumps, and this inhibition is proposed to be released when phospholemman is phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinases (PKAs) (Bibert et al., 2008; Han et al., 2010; Mishra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of phospholemman by PKAs appears to increase the affinity of pumps for cytoplasmic Na.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation of phospholemman by PKAs appears to increase the affinity of pumps for cytoplasmic Na, while phosphorylation of phospholemman by protein kinase Cs (PKCs) increases maximal pump activity (Han et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of phospholemman by protein kinase Cs (PKCs) increases maximal pump activity.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation of phospholemman by PKAs appears to increase the affinity of pumps for cytoplasmic Na, while phosphorylation of phospholemman by protein kinase Cs (PKCs) increases maximal pump activity (Han et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to duplicate results with dyes.
source: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to duplicate results with dyes (Despa et al., 2005), to mildly stimulate pump currents under all experimental conditions (Kockskamper et al., 2000), to have no effect (Ishizuka and Berlin, 1993; Main et al., 1997; Fine et al., 2013), or to inhibit pump currents via an oxidative mechanism (Galougahi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to mildly stimulate pump currents under all experimental conditions.
source: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to duplicate results with dyes (Despa et al., 2005), to mildly stimulate pump currents under all experimental conditions (Kockskamper et al., 2000), to have no effect (Ishizuka and Berlin, 1993; Main et al., 1997; Fine et al., 2013), or to inhibit pump currents via an oxidative mechanism (Galougahi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to have no effect.
source: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to duplicate results with dyes (Despa et al., 2005), to mildly stimulate pump currents under all experimental conditions (Kockskamper et al., 2000), to have no effect (Ishizuka and Berlin, 1993; Main et al., 1997; Fine et al., 2013), or to inhibit pump currents via an oxidative mechanism (Galougahi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to inhibit pump currents via an oxidative mechanism.
source: During whole cell patch clamp of cardiac myocytes, activation of PKAs has been reported to duplicate results with dyes (Despa et al., 2005), to mildly stimulate pump currents under all experimental conditions (Kockskamper et al., 2000), to have no effect (Ishizuka and Berlin, 1993; Main et al., 1997; Fine et al., 2013), or to inhibit pump currents via an oxidative mechanism (Galougahi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: One analysis suggests that phosphorylation by PKA inhibits pump activity in the absence of Ca, but overcomes an inhibitory action of Ca and thereby enhances pump activity in the presence of cytoplasmic Ca.
source: One analysis suggests that phosphorylation by PKA inhibits pump activity in the absence of Ca, but overcomes an inhibitory action of Ca and thereby enhances pump activity, albeit modestly, in the presence of cytoplasmic Ca (Gao et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both small stimulatory effects and inhibitory effects of PKCs on Na/K pumps are reported.
source: Results for PKCs are similarly complex and presumably reflect complexities of PKC signaling in cardiac myocytes. Both small stimulatory effects (Gao et al., 1999; Han et al., 2006) and inhibitory effects (White et al., 2009) are reported, the latter occurring through oxidative stress signaling mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Na/K pumps are evidently regulated by trafficking mechanisms in some cell types.
source: Na/K pumps are evidently regulated by trafficking mechanisms in some cell types (Al-Khalili et al., 2003; Liu and Shapiro, 2007; Lecuona et al., 2009; Alves et al., 2015), but there is little support for physiological regulation of cardiac pumps by these mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is little support for physiological regulation of cardiac pumps by trafficking mechanisms.
source: Na/K pumps are evidently regulated by trafficking mechanisms in some cell types (Al-Khalili et al., 2003; Liu and Shapiro, 2007; Lecuona et al., 2009; Alves et al., 2015), but there is little support for physiological regulation of cardiac pumps by these mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature review.

claim: Nonconventional endocytic mechanisms can remove pumps from the sarcolemma during reperfusion injury.
source: Nonconventional endocytic mechanisms can remove pumps from the sarcolemma during reperfusion injury (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Other mechanisms proposed to regulate the activity of Na/K pumps in cardiac myocytes include redox-dependent glutathionylation of the beta subunits of Na/K pumps.
source: Other mechanisms proposed to regulate the activity of Na/K pumps in cardiac myocytes include redox-dependent glutathionylation of the beta subunits of Na/K pumps (Liu et al., 2012) and the modulation of phospholemman function by palmitoylation (Tulloch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Other mechanisms proposed to regulate the activity of Na/K pumps in cardiac myocytes include the modulation of phospholemman function by palmitoylation.
source: Other mechanisms proposed to regulate the activity of Na/K pumps in cardiac myocytes include redox-dependent glutathionylation of the beta subunits of Na/K pumps (Liu et al., 2012) and the modulation of phospholemman function by palmitoylation (Tulloch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Na/K pump currents can run down during whole-cell patch clamp experiments.
source: Given this background, we initiated a new analysis of pump regulation in murine myocytes, starting with the observation that Na/K pump currents can run down during whole-cell patch clamp experiments.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: A brief elevation of cytoplasmic Ca via reverse Na/Ca exchange had substantially larger effects on pump activity than the activation of either PKAs or PKCs.
source: Attempting to stop and/or reverse this run-down, it became evident that a brief elevation of cytoplasmic Ca via reverse Na/Ca exchange had substantially larger effects on pump activity than the activation of either PKAs or PKCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figures 5-6.

claim: The stimulatory effects of transient Ca elevation occur as an apparent increase of the cytoplasmic Na affinity of Na/K pumps.
source: As described here, the stimulatory effects of transient Ca elevation, usually associated with spontaneous beating, occur as an apparent increase of the cytoplasmic Na affinity of Na/K pumps, the same functional effect proposed to occur with PKA activation (Despa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Subsequent to a transient Ca elevation, peak pump currents activated by extracellular K are strongly enhanced.
source: Subsequent to a transient Ca elevation, peak pump currents activated by extracellular K are strongly enhanced, and the current decay that occurs during continued K application is attenuated.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The current decay that occurs during continued K application is attenuated after transient Ca elevation.
source: Subsequent to a transient Ca elevation, peak pump currents activated by extracellular K are strongly enhanced, and the current decay that occurs during continued K application is attenuated.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Current decay has been ascribed previously to depletion of cytoplasmic Na in a restricted space.
source: This decay has been ascribed previously to depletion of cytoplasmic Na in a restricted space (Fujioka et al.; Su et al., 1998; Verdonck et al., 2004), and we explore here the possibility that current decay reflects instead, or additionally, an inactivation mechanism that bears similarity to the Na-dependent inactivation of Na/Ca exchangers (Hilgemann et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Current decay may reflect an inactivation mechanism that bears similarity to the Na-dependent inactivation of Na/Ca exchangers.
source: This decay has been ascribed previously to depletion of cytoplasmic Na in a restricted space (Fujioka et al.; Su et al., 1998; Verdonck et al., 2004), and we explore here the possibility that current decay reflects instead, or additionally, an inactivation mechanism that bears similarity to the Na-dependent inactivation of Na/Ca exchangers (Hilgemann et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis explored in the study, supported by citation to previous work on Na/Ca exchangers.

claim: Inactivation of Na/K pumps would occur when one or more Na binding sites are unoccupied.
source: In contrast to Na/Ca exchangers, inactivation of Na/K pumps would not occur when cytoplasmic binding sites are occupied by Na. Rather, it would occur when one or more Na binding sites are unoccupied, while recovery from inactivation would be promoted by Na binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Recovery from inactivation would be promoted by Na binding.
source: In contrast to Na/Ca exchangers, inactivation of Na/K pumps would not occur when cytoplasmic binding sites are occupied by Na. Rather, it would occur when one or more Na binding sites are unoccupied, while recovery from inactivation would be promoted by Na binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: No effect of PKA activation was discerned in the absence of Ca elevations.
source: We do not discern any effect of PKA activation in the absence of Ca elevations and the stimulatory effects of Ca elevation occur similarly in phospholemman-deficient myocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The stimulatory effects of Ca elevation occur similarly in phospholemman-deficient myocytes.
source: We do not discern any effect of PKA activation in the absence of Ca elevations and the stimulatory effects of Ca elevation occur similarly in phospholemman-deficient myocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Physical changes of the membrane itself may be involved in Ca-dependent pump regulation, rather than classical signaling mechanisms.
source: Further results suggest that physical changes of the membrane itself may be involved, rather than classical signaling mechanisms, and that Na transporters in close vicinity to one another may interact functionally by modifying physical properties of the adjacent bilayer.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data in Figures 10-12.

claim: Na transporters in close vicinity to one another may interact functionally by modifying physical properties of the adjacent bilayer.
source: Further results suggest that physical changes of the membrane itself may be involved, rather than classical signaling mechanisms, and that Na transporters in close vicinity to one another may interact functionally by modifying physical properties of the adjacent bilayer.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations.

claim: Maximal pump currents are at least 5 pA/pF when pumps are maximally activated by cytoplasmic Na (110 mM) and extracellular K (7 mM).
source: Figure 2A is a representative current record when pumps are maximally activated by cytoplasmic Na (110 mM) and extracellular K (7 mM). Maximal pump currents are at least 5 pA/pF.
evidence: This is directly measured in the experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pump currents typically activate within solution switch times (~100 ms) when maximally activated.
source: The pump currents typically activate within solution switch times (~100 ms) and remain nearly constant during application of extracellular K.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In the presence of cytoplasmic K and with lower cytoplasmic Na concentration, the pump current activated by extracellular K decays over 10 to 15 s.
source: In contrast, Figure 2B is a representative current record using a cytoplasmic solution with 90 mM K and 25 mM Na. In the presence of cytoplasmic K and with this lower cytoplasmic Na concentration, the pump current activated by extracellular K (7 mM) amounts to 2.4 pA/pF and immediately begins to decline, approaching a steady state over 10 to 15 s.
evidence: This is directly observed in Figure 2B.

claim: The decaying current component typically amounts to more than one-half of the peak current.
source: The decaying current component typically amounts to more than one-half of the peak current.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data, e.g., Figure 2B.

claim: Membrane capacitance typically decreases abruptly by 0.5 to 1% upon application of extracellular K.
source: Importantly for our subsequent analysis, membrane capacitance typically decreases abruptly by 0.5 to 1% upon application of extracellular K and then declines further, but to a lesser extent, as pump current falls during K exposure.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental records, e.g., Figure 2B.

claim: Upon removal of K, the capacitance signal returns toward its baseline with a slow multi-second time course that mimics the availability of pump currents for activation by renewed application of extracellular K.
source: Upon removal of K, the capacitance signal returns toward its baseline with a slow multi-second time course that mimics in our experience the availability of pump currents for activation by renewed application of extracellular K.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Pump currents were very effectively inhibited by ouabain (0.3 mM).
source: To test for sensitivity to heart glycosides, the myocyte was moved into two separate solution streams containing ouabain at a concentration that was high enough (0.3 mM) to effectively block rodent Na/K pumps (Herzig and Mohr, 1984). The currents were very effectively inhibited by ouabain (n = 5), demonstrating that they indeed reflect Na/K pump activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B with citation support.

claim: The transient capacitive signals are ablated by ouabain, indicating that they likely arise from Na/K pumps.
source: Importantly, the transient capacitive signals, as well as pump currents, are ablated by ouabain, indicating that they likely arise from Na/K pumps.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The absence of extracellular K will cause pumps to accumulate nearly exclusively in the E2 conformation because the E2 to E1 transition is blocked.
source: As illustrated in the cartoon in Figure 1, the absence of extracellular K will cause pumps to accumulate nearly exclusively in the E2 conformation because the E2 to E1 transition is blocked.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the Na/K pump cycle.

claim: Application of extracellular K allows pumps to cycle between E2 and E1 conformations.
source: Application of extracellular K then allows pumps to cycle between E2 and E1 conformations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the Na/K pump cycle.

claim: All pumps should return to the E2 configuration immediately upon removing extracellular K.
source: However, all pumps should return to the E2 configuration immediately upon removing extracellular K.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the Na/K pump cycle.

claim: The capacitive signal returns immediately to the pre-K value when cytoplasmic Na is high and pump currents are stable.
source: As evident in Figure 2A, the capacitive signal returns immediately to the pre-K value when cytoplasmic Na is high and pump currents are stable.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2A.

claim: The capacitive signals do not immediately return to baseline after removing extracellular K when cytoplasmic Na is submaximal.
source: However, the capacitive signals do not immediately return to baseline after removing extracellular K when cytoplasmic Na is submaximal, as in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2B.

claim: This is a first indication that pumps may become locked into states that cannot cycle during the time in which currents decay.
source: This a first indication that pumps may become locked into states that cannot cycle during the time in which currents decay.
evidence: This is an inference from the capacitance observations.

claim: In the presence of low extracellular Na concentrations (<20 mM), the rapid binding of Na to E2 configurations of the pump gives rise to significant capacitive signals that dissipate when pumps transition from the E2 to the E1 configuration.
source: Concerning the source of these capacitance signals, we have shown previously that in the presence of low extracellular Na concentrations (<20 mM), the rapid binding of Na to E2 configurations of the pump gives rise to significant capacitive signals that dissipate when pumps transition from the E2 to the E1 configuration (Lu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Upon switching extracellular Na from 20 mM to lower concentrations and back to 20 mM, capacitance reversibly decreased and increased within solution switch times by about 0.5%.
source: We verified that Na binding is a major component of these signals as follows: Measurements were initiated with the standard extracellular solution containing 20 mM Na. Upon switching extracellular Na from 20 mM to lower concentrations and back to 20 mM, capacitance reversibly decreased and increased within solution switch times by about 0.5%, as in Figure 2A (5 observations).
evidence: This is experimental verification performed in the study.

claim: In the presence of 90 mM K, the K50 for peak current is 19 mM Na and the Hill coefficient is 2.4.
source: (C) In the presence of 90 mM K, the K50 for peak current is 19 mM Na and the Hill coefficient is 2.4, while the 10 s current shows a K50 of 30 mM and Hill slope of 2.6.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of 90 mM K, the 10 s current shows a K50 of 30 mM and Hill slope of 2.6.
source: (C) In the presence of 90 mM K, the K50 for peak current is 19 mM Na and the Hill coefficient is 2.4, while the 10 s current shows a K50 of 30 mM and Hill slope of 2.6.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: In the absence of cytoplasmic K, peak currents are best described by a Hill equation with a K50 of 6 mM cytoplasmic Na and a Hill slope of 1.6.
source: (D) In the absence of cytoplasmic K, peak currents are best described by a Hill equation with a K50 of 6 mM cytoplasmic Na and a Hill slope of 1.6.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: In the absence of cytoplasmic K, the 10 s current is shifted to a K50 of 37 mM with a Hill slope of 1.1.
source: The 10 s current is shifted to a K50 of 37 mM with a Hill slope of 1.1
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: Although currents are smaller in the presence of cytoplasmic K, the fractional decay of current is greater at all Na concentrations.
source: Although currents are smaller in the presence of cytoplasmic K, the fractional decay of current is greater at all Na concentrations.
evidence: This is observed by comparing data in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: At 23°C, pump currents are at least 4-times smaller than at 37°C.
source: At the lower temperature, pump currents are at least 4-times smaller than at 37°C.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data comparing Figures 2C-D with 2E.

claim: At 23°C, the half maximal pump currents occurred at 4.1 and 21 mM Na for peak and 15 s currents, respectively.
source: Fitting the composite results for peak and 15 s currents to Hill functions, the half maximal pump currents occurred at 4.1 and 21 mM Na, respectively, and Hill slopes were 1.7 and 1.1, respectively, for peak and 15 s currents.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: At 23°C, Hill slopes were 1.7 and 1.1 for peak and 15 s currents, respectively.
source: Fitting the composite results for peak and 15 s currents to Hill functions, the half maximal pump currents occurred at 4.1 and 21 mM Na, respectively, and Hill slopes were 1.7 and 1.1, respectively, for peak and 15 s currents.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: The fractional decay of pump currents increases monotonically with decreasing Na concentration and is reasonably described by a simple reciprocal hyperbola with a Kd of 12 mM.
source: The fractional decay of pump currents, plotted in Figure 2F, increases monotonically with decreasing Na concentration and is reasonably described by a simple reciprocal hyperbola, Kd/(Kd+Nai), with a Kd of 12 mM.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data in Figure 2F.

claim: Values obtained for the cytoplasmic Na mixing volume are about 10% of the expected cytoplasmic volumes of murine myocytes.
source: As described next, values obtained for the cytoplasmic Na mixing volume are about 10% of the expected cytoplasmic volumes of murine myocytes (Stagg et al., 2004), and the apparent exchange times to this restricted volume are on the order of 2 to 3 s.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data with citation to expected volumes.

claim: The apparent exchange times to the restricted volume are on the order of 2 to 3 s.
source: As described next, values obtained for the cytoplasmic Na mixing volume are about 10% of the expected cytoplasmic volumes of murine myocytes (Stagg et al., 2004), and the apparent exchange times to this restricted volume are on the order of 2 to 3 s.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The peak Na/K pump currents were about five-fold smaller at 23°C than at 37°C.
source: As tabulated in Figure 3C, the peak Na/K pump currents were about five-fold smaller at 23°C than at 37°C.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: The fractional decay of current was very similar at 23°C and 37°C (0.67 versus 0.65).
source: The fractional decay of current was however very similar (0.67 versus 0.65), while the decay time constant was larger and the apparent Na mixing volume was smaller at the lower temperature.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: With 25 mM cytoplasmic Na, peak currents are increased by about 30% in the absence of cytoplasmic K compared to with K.
source: With 25 mM cytoplasmic Na, peak currents are increased by about 30%, whereas the fractional decay of current is decreased from 0.65 to 0.52.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: The fractional decay of current is decreased from 0.65 to 0.52 in the absence of cytoplasmic K.
source: With 25 mM cytoplasmic Na, peak currents are increased by about 30%, whereas the fractional decay of current is decreased from 0.65 to 0.52.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: With 40 mM Li in the pipette solution, small pump currents (<0.5 pA/pF) could be activated by application of extracellular K.
source: With 40 mM Li in the pipette solution (30 mM TEA, 70 mM NMG, and no K), small pump currents (<0.5 pA/pF) could be activated by application of extracellular K.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: Pump currents with Li showed unusually strong decay (>90%) in spite of their small magnitude.
source: These currents showed unusually strong decay (>90%) in spite of their small magnitude, such that the apparent mixing volume of Li would be substantially less than a picoliter.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3C.

claim: This result is consistent with the inactivation model because more binding sites will be empty with a low affinity pump ligand, thereby promoting inactivation.
source: This result is consistent with the inactivation model because more binding sites will be empty with a low affinity pump ligand, thereby promoting inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation with Li.

claim: Outward Na/Ca exchange current is suppressed immediately after a period of high Na/K pump activity.
source: As verified in Figure 13A, and as expected for depletion of cytoplasmic Na, outward Na/Ca exchange current (i.e. Na efflux driven by Ca influx) is suppressed immediately after a period of high Na/K pump activity, and exchange current recovers with a time course that is similar to the recovery of pump currents .
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 13A.

claim: Exchange current recovers with a time course that is similar to the recovery of pump currents.
source: As verified in Figure 13A, and as expected for depletion of cytoplasmic Na, outward Na/Ca exchange current (i.e. Na efflux driven by Ca influx) is suppressed immediately after a period of high Na/K pump activity, and exchange current recovers with a time course that is similar to the recovery of pump currents .
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 13A.

claim: Exchange currents were decreased immediately after the pump current transient by a fractional amount that was about one-half of the fractional decay of pump current.
source: Exchange currents were decreased immediately after the pump current transient by a fractional amount that was about one-half of the fractional decay of pump current.
evidence: This is observed in the experiments described for Figure 13A.

claim: Based on pump currents, the apparent volume in which Na depletion would be taking place amounted to 2.2 ± 0.5 pL (n=9).
source: Based on pump currents, the apparent volume in which Na depletion would be taking place amounted to 2.2 ± 0.5 pL (n=9).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: As cytoplasmic Na is increased from 0 to 100 mM, the rate constant that best describes pump current decay increases to a maximum with nearly the same Na dependence as pump current itself.
source: In equivalent experiments using rat myocytes, Verdonck et al. described that as cytoplasmic Na is increased from 0 to 100 mM, the rate constant that best describes pump current decay increases to a maximum with nearly the same Na dependence as pump current itself (Verdonck et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: This result seems inconsistent with the Na depletion model.
source: This result seems inconsistent with the Na depletion model.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited result.

claim: If current decay were occurring as a result of Na depletion, the rate constant should have decreased as Na was increased above the half-maximal Na concentration of 8 mM and up to 100 mM.
source: If current decay were occurring as a result of Na depletion, the rate constant should have decreased as Na was increased above the half-maximal Na concentration of 8 mM and up to 100 mM.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what the depletion model would predict.

claim: The result supports an inactivation model in which the Na binding to inactive states promote recovery from inactivation.
source: Rather, the result supports an inactivation model in which the Na binding to inactive states promote recovery from inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited kinetic result.

claim: In experiments at 23°C, the initial rate of pump current decay increased as cytoplasmic Na was decreased from 0.06 ± 0.02 s−1 at 40 mM Na to 0.14 ± 0.02 s−1 at 2.5 mM Na.
source: In the experiments described in Figure 2 at 23°C, the initial rate of pump current decay increased as cytoplasmic Na was decreased from 0.06 ± 0.02 s−1 at 40 mM Na to 0.14 ± 0.02 s−1 at 2.5 mM Na.
evidence: This is determined from experimental data.

claim: This favors the suggestion that inactivation occurs preferentially from E1 states that are not fully occupied by Na.
source: This favors our suggestion that inactivation occurs preferentially from E1 states that are not fully occupied by Na.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic data.

claim: Just 5 mM Na in the extracellular solution without K suppresses for the most part an outward current that is very likely activated by contaminating K in nominally Na-free solutions.
source: In describing the effects of extracellular Na on Na/K pump currents, we document first that just 5 mM Na in the extracellular solution without K suppresses for the most part an outward current that is very likely activated by contaminating K in nominally Na-free solutions, similar to results for squid axons (Rakowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A with citation support.

claim: When 5 mM Na is replaced with 5 mM NMG, a small outward current develops that decays partially over 20 s.
source: When 5 mM Na is replaced with 5 mM NMG, a small outward current develops that decays partially over 20 s, as expected for a pump current, and application of 5 mM K then activates a maximal pump current that is less than half of the previous pump currents.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Application of 5 mM K activates a maximal pump current that is less than half of the previous pump currents after Na removal.
source: When 5 mM Na is replaced with 5 mM NMG, a small outward current develops that decays partially over 20 s, as expected for a pump current, and application of 5 mM K then activates a maximal pump current that is less than half of the previous pump currents.

Application of extracellular Na under conditions that promote accumulation of cytoplasmic ADP suppresses the transient phase of pump currents, such that pump currents activate to approximately their quasi steady state (15 s) magnitude without a peak followed by current decay (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C (note: text says Figure 5 but should be Figure 4C based on content).

claim: A large, continuous Na influx via forward Na/Ca exchange fails to enhance pump currents, although the operation of pumps can depress reverse exchange currents.
source: (7) A large, continuous Na influx via forward Na/Ca exchange fails to enhance pump currents, although the operation of pumps can depress reverse exchange currents (Figure 13B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 13B.

claim: The fractional decay of pump currents often increases as currents decline over time, a behavior that is opposite to the pattern expected for an ion depletion mechanism.
source: (8) The fractional decay of pump currents often increases as currents decline over time, a behavior that is opposite to the pattern expected for an ion depletion mechanism (e.g. Figure 11).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11.

claim: The rate of pump current decay does not decrease as cytoplasmic Na is increased into the saturation range for pump activity.
source: Finally, as noted in Results, the rate of pump current decay does not decrease as cytoplasmic Na is increased into the saturation range for pump activity (Verdonck et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: During a maintained average pump current of 300 pA, about 2 mmole ATP per liter cytoplasm will be cleaved every 10 s in a 20 pL cell.
source: During a maintained average pump current of 300 pA, about 2 mmole ATP per liter cytoplasm will be cleaved every 10 s in a 20 pL cell.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental conditions.

claim: In the physiological setting, nucleotide changes must be very rapidly countered by ATP regeneration via glycolysis and/or oxidative phosphorylation.
source: In the physiological setting, these nucleotide changes must be very rapidly countered by ATP regeneration via glycolysis and/or oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on physiological knowledge.

claim: Extensive local depletion of ATP might be an immediate cause of pump current decay during metabolic stress.
source: On the one hand, extensive local depletion of ATP might be an immediate cause of pump current decay during metabolic stress.
evidence: This is speculation.

claim: ADP accumulation during metabolic stress will favor occupancy of states that can inactivate.
source: On the other hand, our work suggests that ADP accumulation during metabolic stress will favor occupancy of states that can inactivate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: It appears that significant membrane changes are occurring rapidly in the presence of metabolic stress.
source: Independent of Na/K pump function, it appears that significant membrane changes are occurring rapidly in the presence of metabolic stress (Figure 11).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11.

claim: Transient elevations of cytoplasmic Ca have two effects when cytoplasmic Na is non-saturating: Ca elevation decreases the Na/K pump current decay and increases peak pump currents.
source: Transient elevations of cytoplasmic Ca have two effects when cytoplasmic Na is non-saturating. Ca elevation decreases the Na/K pump current decay and increases peak pump currents (Figures 6–10 and Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in multiple figures.

claim: A genuine increase of Na/K pump Na affinity will cause an increase of peak pump currents when extracellular K is applied.
source: In both a 'Na depletion' model and an 'inactivation' model, a genuine increase of Na/K pump Na affinity will of course cause an increase of peak pump currents when extracellular K is applied.
evidence: This is a logical inference about model predictions.

claim: A genuine increase of Na affinity can explain changes of pump current decay that occur.
source: Qualitatively, a genuine increase of Na affinity can also explain changes of pump current decay that occur.
evidence: This is a logical inference.

claim: In a depletion model, cytoplasmic Na must decrease more extensively to cause a fall of pump current when the Na affinity is increased.
source: In a depletion model, cytoplasmic Na must decrease more extensively to cause a fall of pump current when the Na affinity is increased.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the depletion model.

claim: In an inactivation model, a higher Na affinity attenuates inactivation because the number of E1 pumps without a bound Na would be decreased.
source: In an inactivation model, a higher Na affinity attenuates inactivation because the number of E1 pumps without a bound Na would be decreased.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the inactivation model.

claim: The existence of a labile, hydrophobic Na antagonist would go quite far to explain many results.
source: In this context, the existence of a labile, hydrophobic Na antagonist would go quite far to explain many results.
evidence: This is speculation.

claim: It is not necessary to evoke a genuine change of Na affinity to explain these results.
source: Nevertheless, it is not necessary to evoke a genuine change of Na affinity to explain these results.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative interpretation.

claim: One possible extension of the inactivation model is that pumps inactivate at multiple points in the pump cycle, including E2 states.
source: One possible extension of the inactivation model is that pumps inactivate at multiple points in the pump cycle, including E2 states.
evidence: This is speculation about model extensions.

claim: If transient Ca elevation favors the recovery from multiple inactive states, peak pump currents will increase without evoking a genuine increase of Na affinity.
source: If transient Ca elevation favors the recovery from multiple inactive states, not just those immediately coupled to E1 conformations, peak pump currents will increase without evoking a genuine increase of Na affinity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model.

claim: In a recent study employing rabbit cardiac myocytes, Na/K pump current decay during application of extracellular K was implicated to involve the glutathionylation of Na/K pump beta subunits.
source: In a recent study employing rabbit cardiac myocytes, Na/K pump current decay during application of extracellular K was implicated to involve the glutathionylation of Na/K pump beta subunits (Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Results with mouse myocytes are very different from rabbit myocytes, and current decay in mouse myocytes is much faster than in rabbit myocytes.
source: For unknown reasons, our equivalent results with mouse myocytes are very different, and we stress that current decay in mouse myocytes is much faster than in rabbit myocytes.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the data.

claim: Experimental results for routine protocols are similar in myocytes from mice lacking Peroxyredoxin6.
source: Experimental results for our routine protocols are similar in myocytes from mice lacking Peroxyredoxin6 and in which turnover of oxidized glutathione to glutathione should be decreased (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with citation support.

claim: Experiments employing high concentrations of cytoplasmic glutathione, oxidized glutathione, superoxide dismutase, and reducing agents give no indication that redox-dependent processes are immediately involved in the effects of Ca elevations or their reversal.
source: Experiments employing high concentrations of cytoplasmic glutathione (>5 mM), oxidized glutathione (>5 mM), superoxide dismutase, and reducing agents give no indication that redox-dependent processes are immediately involved in the effects of Ca elevations or their reversal (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Efforts to identify specific molecular mechanisms by which Ca elevation modulate Na/K pump activity are to date unsuccessful.
source: Our efforts to identify specific molecular mechanisms by which Ca elevation modulate Na/K pump activity are to date unsuccessful (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental efforts.

claim: These negative outcomes suggest that important Ca-dependent regulatory systems remain to be elucidated in cardiac myocytes.
source: These negative outcomes beg the suggestion that important Ca-dependent regulatory systems remain to be elucidated in cardiac myocytes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the negative results.

claim: It may be an important clue that Ca elevation and Na pump inactivation cause significant but opposite physical changes of the bulk surface membrane, as detected with hydrophobic ions.
source: It may be an important 'clue' that Ca elevation and Na pump inactivation cause significant but opposite physical changes of the bulk surface membrane, as detected with hydrophobic ions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The effects of Ca elevation in intact myocytes have no clear parallels in biochemical pump studies.
source: Further, it appears important that the effects of Ca elevation in intact myocytes have no clear parallels in biochemical pump studies.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Comparable effects of cytoplasmic Ca on Na/K pump currents have never been observed in giant excised membrane patches.
source: And finally, we stress that we have never observed comparable effects of cytoplasmic Ca on Na/K pump currents in giant excised membrane patches in which pump currents appear to be highly activated in comparison to pump currents in intact cells (Lu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citation.

claim: One reason could be that giant excised patches are highly stretched membranes which probably lack actin membrane cytoskeleton.
source: One reason could be that giant excised patches are highly stretched membranes which probably lack actin membrane cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is speculation.

claim: Pump currents in excised patches routinely show an initial 'run-up' that is consistent with the irreversible loss of an endogenous pump inhibitor.
source: On the other hand, pump currents in excised patches routinely show an initial 'run-up' that is consistent with the irreversible loss of an endogenous pump inhibitor (Hilgemann, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: With certainty, critical factors are disrupted or lost when membranes are isolated.
source: With certainty, critical factors are disrupted or lost when membranes are isolated.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences between intact cells and excised patches.

claim: Three parallel changes of Na/K pump and Na/Ca exchange activities can be tracked by a nonselective membrane probe, C6-TPP.
source: Our data reveal three parallel changes of Na/K pump and Na/Ca exchange activities that can be tracked by a nonselective membrane probe, C6-TPP:
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: In response to a transient Ca elevation, both pump currents and exchange currents usually become facilitated.
source: (1) In response to a transient Ca elevation, both pump currents and exchange currents usually become facilitated (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In response to repeated transient Ca elevations, both pump and exchange currents become suppressed and/or are ablated.
source: (2) In response to repeated transient Ca elevations, both currents become suppressed and/or are ablated (Figure 8C and 10A).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 8C and 10A.

claim: Na/K pump current decay during application of extracellular K is associated with a substantial decline of Na/Ca exchange current.
source: (3) Na/K pump current decay during application of extracellular K is associated with a substantial decline of Na/Ca exchange current (Figure 13A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 13A.

claim: The fact that membrane probes sense all three events supports speculation that the three events are related.
source: The fact that membrane probes sense all three events supports speculation that the three events are related.
evidence: This is speculation based on the parallel observations.

claim: Increases of membrane capacitance that occur very reliably after Ca elevations indicate that membrane fusion events are occurring and/or that the membrane is becoming slightly thinner.
source: Increases of membrane capacitance that occur very reliably after Ca elevations (Figures 6,9,10) indicate that membrane fusion events are occurring and/or that the membrane is becoming slightly thinner.
evidence: This is inferred from the capacitance changes.

claim: Since maximal pump currents are not increased by transient Ca elevation, insertion of pumps is not a viable explanation for the activation of pump currents.
source: Since maximal pump currents are not increased by transient Ca elevation (Figure 6B), insertion of pumps is not a viable explanation for the activation of pump currents.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 6B.

claim: Ca-dependent fusion events could bring into the cell surface proteins that subsequently mediate pump activation.
source: However, Ca-dependent fusion events could bring into the cell surface proteins that subsequently mediate pump activation.
evidence: This is speculation.

claim: The parallel increase of hydrophobic ion signals indicates that physical properties of the membrane are indeed changing.
source: The parallel increase of hydrophobic ion signals (Figure 1) indicates that physical properties of the membrane are indeed changing.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 10.

claim: Ca-dependent enzymes that might mediate membrane changes include PLA2s, diacylglycerol kinases, and acyl transferases that generate acyl-phosphatidylethanolamine.
source: Ca-dependent enzymes that might mediate such changes include PLA2s (Brown et al., 2003), diacylglycerol kinases (Sakane and Kanoh, 1997), and acyl transferases that generate acyl-phosphatidylethanolamine (Ogura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation with citation support.

claim: Cardiac (NCX1) Na/Ca exchangers have a large cytoplasmic regulatory domain with multiple Ca binding sites that effectively responds to changes of the time integral of cytoplasmic free Ca.
source: Cardiac (NCX1) Na/Ca exchangers have a large cytoplasmic regulatory domain with multiple Ca binding sites that effectively responds to changes of the time integral of cytoplasmic free Ca (Matsuoka, 1993).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Both conformational changes per se of the NCX1 cytoplasmic domain and its activating influence on Na/Ca exchange function can persist for longer than one minute after cytoplasmic Ca declines.
source: Both conformational changes per se of this domain (John et al., 2011) and its activating influence on Na/Ca exchange function (Hilgemann et al., 1992a) can persist for longer than one minute after cytoplasmic Ca declines.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The cytoplasmic NCX1 domain is one potential Ca sensor for the activation of Na/K pumps by Ca elevation.
source: Thus, the cytoplasmic NCX1 domain is one potential Ca sensor for the activation of Na/K pumps by Ca elevation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of NCX1.

claim: Conformational information would be transferred to Na/K pumps via cytoskeleton, the bilayer, and/or an enzymatic activity.
source: Conformational information would be transferred to Na/K pumps via cytoskeleton, the bilayer, and/or an enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is speculation.

claim: The existence of physical interactions between neighboring transporters is an attractive explanation for findings that specific Na/K pump isoforms regulate cardiac excitation-contraction coupling in a specific manner.
source: The existence of physical interactions between neighboring transporters, independent of Na concentration changes, is an attractive explanation for findings that specific Na/K pump isoforms regulate cardiac excitation-contraction coupling in a specific manner (Rindler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation with citation support.

claim: The physical basis of a restricted subsarcolemmal Na space with multi-second Na exchange remains to be established.
source: As concerns the Na depletion hypothesis, the physical basis of a restricted subsarcolemmal Na space with multi-second Na exchange remains to be established.
evidence: This is stated as an unresolved issue.

claim: Results do not at this time rigorously exclude the existence of a restricted subsarcolemmal Na space.
source: We stress that our results do not at this time rigorously exclude its existence.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: New model systems are now essential to resolve many questions opened by this study.
source: New model systems, which can mimic the functions of Na/K pumps in intact myocytes, are now essential to resolve many questions opened by this study.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.

claim: Ca elevations modulate cardiac Na/K pump activities more powerfully than any conventional signaling pathway in the authors' experience.
source: Surprisingly, Ca elevations modulate cardiac Na/K pump activities more powerfully than any conventional signaling pathway in our experience.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: The underlying mechanisms result in physical changes of the membrane that can be detected by multiple nonspecific membrane probes.
source: The underlying mechanisms result in physical changes of the membrane that can be detected by multiple nonspecific membrane probes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 10-12.

claim: The Ca-dependent mechanisms that modulate Na/K pumps may also modulate the function of Na/Ca exchangers.
source: The Ca-dependent mechanisms that modulate Na/K pumps may also modulate the function of Na/Ca exchangers, and the involvement of membrane per se suggests that other membrane-coupled processes might also be affected.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The involvement of membrane per se suggests that other membrane-coupled processes might also be affected.
source: The Ca-dependent mechanisms that modulate Na/K pumps may also modulate the function of Na/Ca exchangers, and the involvement of membrane per se suggests that other membrane-coupled processes might also be affected.
evidence: This is speculation.
